mcqs.question: Why can't a pure key-value store efficiently answer "give me all sessions belonging to user 42"?
options: The store's interface only supports get/put/delete by exact key, with no concept of querying by anything other than the key itself
Key-value stores have a hard limit of one value per key across the whole database
This kind of query requires a graph database specifically
Key-value stores cannot store more than one session per user
mcqs.explanation: A key-value interface has no query language beyond exact-key lookup, so anything requiring a scan or filter across values isn't supported without a different structure (like a secondary index the key-value store doesn't provide). There's no such one-value-per-key limit, this doesn't require a graph database specifically, and multiple sessions per user is fine, just not queryable this way.

mcqs.question: What lets a document database run `db.products.find({"category": "electronics", "price": {"$lt": 500}})` efficiently, that a pure key-value store cannot do at all?
options: The document store can build secondary indexes on fields inside the document's structure, not just on the outer key
Document stores compress values more efficiently than key-value stores
Document stores always keep the entire collection in memory
The query syntax is simpler, which is the only real difference
mcqs.explanation: Because the database understands the document's internal structure, it can index and filter on nested fields directly — something an opaque-value key-value store has no mechanism for. Compression and in-memory storage aren't the distinguishing factor, and the difference is capability, not just syntax simplicity.

mcqs.question: A team embeds every comment directly into its blog post document, and popular posts start loading slowly. What's the underlying mistake?
options: MongoDB documents cannot contain arrays at all
Embedding a collection with no natural size cap (comments can grow unbounded) forces the whole growing array to load and rewrite on every read/write
The blog post collection needs a secondary index on the title field
Comments should always be stored in Redis instead of any document store
mcqs.explanation: The problem is embedding an unbounded child collection — as comments accumulate, the document grows large and every read/write touches that growing array. MongoDB does support arrays, a title index wouldn't fix this, and Redis isn't the required fix; referencing comments in their own collection is.

mcqs.question: Why does DynamoDB single-table design require knowing your access patterns before designing the table, unlike a typical relational schema?
options: DynamoDB has no query language at all
DynamoDB requires all tables to have exactly one column
DynamoDB has no cross-table joins, so every query must be servable by a single partition-key lookup or sort-key range — the key structure has to encode the access pattern in advance
Relational databases also require this; it's not actually a difference
mcqs.explanation: Without joins, the only way to serve a query efficiently is to have designed the partition/sort keys so that query is a single partition read — meaning access patterns must be known upfront. DynamoDB does have a query language, doesn't restrict tables to one column, and this genuinely differs from relational modeling, which can defer query design.

mcqs.question: Why is Redis chosen for session lookups and feature-flag checks that run on nearly every request, instead of querying the primary relational database directly?
options: Redis guarantees stronger durability than any relational database
Redis supports more complex queries than SQL
Redis's in-memory GET typically completes in under 1ms versus several to tens of milliseconds for a relational query, and it also removes that load from the primary database
Relational databases cannot store session data in any form
mcqs.explanation: The latency gap plus offloading traffic from the primary is the real reason — Redis is fast because it's in-memory and looked up by exact key, not because it has richer querying or stronger durability by default. Relational databases can absolutely store session data; it's just usually slower per lookup at this frequency.

mcqs.question: A team keeps their exact relational schema but stores each table as a separate MongoDB collection, joining them in application code. What do they lose without gaining?
options: They gain single-fetch reads while losing nothing
MongoDB automatically converts this into an optimized single-table design
There is no real downside to this approach

They keep relational-style join complexity, but now it runs slower in application code without a query planner or foreign-key constraints, without gaining the document store's single-fetch read benefit
mcqs.explanation: This approach inherits joins' complexity without a query planner or referential integrity, and doesn't get the aggregate-read benefit that justifies using a document store in the first place — the worst of both worlds. MongoDB doesn't auto-convert this, and there is a real, well-documented downside.
